blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify the conditions of supply, and show how a change in one shifts the supply curve.

blocks.heading: The conditions of supply
blocks.text: The conditions of supply are the influences on supply other than the good's own price. The list to know: the costs of the inputs used to make the good; the technology of production; indirect taxes on the good and subsidies for producing it; the prices of other goods the producer could make instead; the weather, for farm and fishing goods; and the number of sellers. The good's own price stays off the list, because it moves the market along the curve.

blocks.heading: A cost fall shifts the curve
blocks.text: Start with a condition: the price of vinyl falls for Namib Signs, a sign-painting firm in Windhoek, while its price per sign stays at N$150. Because printing becomes cheaper at each price, this causes the firm to offer more signs at N$150: 60 a month instead of 40. The whole supply curve shifts right: an increase in supply, meaning more is offered at every price. A rise in an input cost would shift it left: a decrease in supply.

blocks.heading: Weather on the harvest
blocks.text: The weather is a condition of supply for farm goods. Good rains round Otavi raise the maize offered at each price; drought shrinks it, shifting the curve left. Rice farmers in Vietnam watch the same condition: a strong Mekong delta harvest shifts their market's supply curve right, a weak one left. In each case the good's own price has not changed - the whole relationship between price and quantity has.

blocks.heading: Technology, taxes, other goods and the number of sellers
blocks.text:
Technology and productivity. A new machine or method that lets each worker or each hectare produce more lowers the cost of each unit. Producing becomes more worthwhile at every price, so supply increases and the curve shifts right. A bakery in Ongwediva that replaces hand-mixing with an electric mixer can bake 600 loaves a day with the same staff instead of 400, and offers more bread at each price. A fall in productivity, such as when machines break down or many workers fall ill, has the opposite effect.

Indirect taxes and subsidies. An indirect tax, such as a duty charged on each litre of a soft drink, is paid to the government on each unit sold, so it works like an extra cost: at every price the producer keeps less, supply decreases and the curve shifts left. A subsidy is a payment from the government to the producer for each unit, which works like a cost cut: supply increases and the curve shifts right. Topic 2.11 follows what each does to the market price.

Prices of other goods the producer could make. Many producers can switch resources between products. A farmer near Mariental can plant his irrigated land with lucerne or with maize. If the price of lucerne rises sharply, lucerne becomes the more rewarding use of the land, so he tends to plant more lucerne and less maize: the supply of maize decreases at every maize price, although the maize price itself has not changed. A fall in the price of the alternative works the other way.

The number of sellers. Market supply adds up what every seller offers at each price. When new firms enter - three new kapana stands open at a taxi rank, or new fishing companies are granted quotas - more is offered at every price and market supply increases. When firms leave, as when a factory closes, market supply decreases and the curve shifts left. In Germany, the many households and farms that began selling electricity from rooftop solar panels after 2000 added to the supply of electricity in this way.

blocks.heading: Movement or shift
blocks.text: The confusion learners make: a price change and a condition change are both written as "supply changed". The boundary: the good's own price moves the market along the curve; a condition of supply, with the price unchanged, shifts the whole curve. The test: whether the good's own price changed. Where it did, the diagram shows an extension or a contraction along the curve; where it did not, a shift.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 2.5 traces what these shifts do to the market price, and topic 2.8 asks how strongly quantity supplied responds to price.
